cards.title: What data entry is — turning messy paper into clean records
cards.takeaway: Data entry means typing real-world facts (names, sales, stock, dates) accurately into a spreadsheet or database so a business can trust its numbers.
cards.body:
Every shop, clinic, school, and company runs on information. When receipts sit in a nylon bag, nobody knows total profit!

- **Data entry:** Accurately capturing and typing raw facts into structured rows and columns.
- **Data management:** Organising, backing up, securing, and analysing those records over time.

cards.title: The 4 core data types every spreadsheet uses
cards.takeaway: Every cell you type belongs to one of four main types: Text, Numbers, Dates, or Currency (percentages are just a way of showing numbers!).
cards.body:
Spreadsheets treat cells differently depending on their **data type**:
1. **Text:** Names, addresses, product titles, and **phone numbers** (e.g. `Chinedu Okafor`, `08031234567` — stored as text so the leading `0` does not vanish!).
2. **Numbers:** Quantities, scores, ages (`12`, `450`).
3. **Dates:** Calendar days (`29/10/2026`).
4. **Currency:** Money amounts (`₦15,000.00`).

*Watch out:* **Percentages** are a number display format, **not** one of the four main data types!

check.prompt: What are the FOUR main data types taught in data entry?
check.hint: Remember the trap: percentages are just a number format — money is the fourth main type!
check.explanation: Spot on! The four main data types are Text, Numbers, Dates, and Currency.

cards.title: The Nigerian date rule: `DD/MM/YYYY`
cards.takeaway: In Nigeria (and the UK), always write Day first, Month second, and 4-digit Year third — like 29/10/2026.
cards.body:
Mixing up day and month is one of the costliest data mistakes in offices!
- **Standard Nigerian format:** **`DD/MM/YYYY`** (for example, `05/11/2026` means 5th November 2026, **not** May 11th).
- Always use a **4-digit year** (`2026`, not `26`) so there is zero confusion.

cards.title: Why you NEVER type the `₦` symbol or commas by hand!
cards.takeaway: Type plain digits like 15000 into the cell, then apply Currency formatting — typing '₦15,000' by hand turns it into text that Excel cannot add!
cards.body:
Here is the #1 beginner mistake in Excel:
- If you manually type `₦15,000` with the Naira sign, Excel often treats the cell as **Text** (a word) instead of a **Number**!
- When you later run `=SUM(...)`, Excel ignores text cells and your total comes out wrong!

**The professional rule:**
1. Type **plain digits only**: `15000`
2. Select the column and choose **Currency (`₦`)** format so Excel displays `₦15,000` while keeping real math underneath!

check.prompt: Your friend typed '₦15,000' by hand into Excel and says SUM refuses to add it. Why?

choices.text: Excel cannot calculate Naira amounts above 10,000
Typing the ₦ symbol manually made Excel store it as Text; enter 15000 and apply Currency formatting instead
They forgot to restart the computer after typing
Numbers must always be typed in capital letters

check.hint: Excel can only add real numbers — symbols typed by hand turn numbers into text strings.
check.explanation: Exactly! Always enter raw digits (`15000`) and let Excel's Currency format add the `₦` and comma visually.

cards.title: Clean formatting for names and phone numbers
cards.takeaway: Write names in Title Case ('Ngozi Eze') and format phone columns as Text so the starting zero in 0803... stays intact.
cards.body:
Two small habits instantly make your sheet look like a pro built it:
- **Names in Title Case:** Write `Ngozi Eze` — not `ngozi eze` and not `NGOZI EZE`.
- **Phone numbers (digits only, Text format):** Format the column as **Text** (or start with an apostrophe `'08031234567`) so Excel keeps the leading `0` and remove random spaces or dashes.

cards.title: Accuracy beats raw speed every time
cards.takeaway: One wrong zero turns ₦50,000 into ₦500,000 — check headers, keep one fact per column, and verify totals.
cards.body:
Before submitting any sheet, run a 30-second visual check:
- Numbers & currency naturally align to the **right** side of an Excel cell.
- Text naturally aligns to the **left** side.
- If one price suddenly hugs the **left** edge of its cell, Excel thinks it is **Text** — fix it immediately!

check.prompt: What is the standard date format used across Nigerian businesses and government forms?
check.hint: In Nigeria we say '29th of October, 2026' — Day, Month, full Year.
check.explanation: Correct! DD/MM/YYYY (for example, 29/10/2026) is the standard Nigerian date format.

cards.title: Seeing `#####` in a cell? Don't panic!
cards.takeaway: `#####` only means the column is too narrow to show the full number or date — double-click the column border to widen it.
cards.body:
New learners often think `#####` means they broke a formula. Good news: your data is completely safe!
- Move your mouse between the column letters at the top (e.g. between `C` and `D`).
- **Double-click** that line, and the column widens automatically to fit every digit.

check.prompt: Why did `08031234567` turn into `8031234567` (missing the first zero) when typed into a plain cell, and how do you fix it?

choices.text: Excel treated it as a math number and dropped the leading zero; format the column as Text first
The zero key on the keyboard is broken
Nigerian phone numbers are only 10 digits
Format the phone number as Currency

check.hint: In math, 08 equals 8 — so phone numbers should be stored as Text, not math numbers.
check.explanation: Spot on! Formatting phone columns as Text preserves the leading zero because you never do arithmetic on a phone number.
